domain: Viewport, layout, safe areas, on-screen keyboard and scrolling

items.title: Viewport meta baseline for app-like pages
items.what: One viewport meta that turns off the 980px virtual viewport, starts at 100% zoom, lets the page draw edge to edge, and on Android shrinks the layout for the on-screen keyboard.
items.why: Without it the page renders zoomed out or letterboxed around the notch, and a bottom composer or tab bar disappears under the keyboard. With it, Android behaves like a native resizing window with no JS, and iOS gets full-bleed drawing plus safe-area values.
items.how:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover, interactive-widget=resizes-content">

<!-- width=device-width : layout width = device width (media queries work)
     initial-scale=1     : don't auto-zoom-out when something overflows
     viewport-fit=cover  : draw under notch / home indicator / Android gesture bar; env(safe-area-inset-*) become non-zero, so you must pad with them
     interactive-widget=resizes-content : Android shrinks the layout viewport (and vh/dvh/%) for the keyboard -->
items.support: width/initial-scale: every mobile browser; desktop browsers ignore the meta. viewport-fit: Safari iOS 11+, Chrome Android 135+ (BCD; tied to edge-to-edge), Firefox Android 79+. interactive-widget: Chrome Android 108+, Firefox Android 133+ (BCD), Samsung 21+, Android WebView 108+. Safari iOS (tab and home-screen app) and every iOS browser (all WebKit): not supported as of Safari 27.0. WebKit landed it in source in Aug 2026, but it is not in Safari or STP yet.
items.gotchas: Unknown keys are ignored, so the same tag is safe on iOS. iOS still needs the visualViewport fix (see the iOS keyboard item). resizes-content relayouts on every keyboard show/hide, and ALL viewport units (vh/svh/lvh/dvh) shrink with the keyboard on Android, so anything sized in vh shrinks too. Chrome 108+ and Firefox Android 132+ default to resizes-visual, so set it explicitly. overlays-content only makes sense if you then lay out around the keyboard yourself (VirtualKeyboard API / keyboard-inset-*). Never add maximum-scale or user-scalable (see the zoom item). Don't add height=device-height. Unit-test layout code that assumes one behaviour per platform, and make code that measures the keyboard tolerate both.

items.title: Never disable zoom (no maximum-scale / user-scalable=no)
items.what: Keep pinch-zoom available. Fix the problems people try to solve with zoom-blocking (focus zoom, double-tap zoom) with targeted CSS instead.
items.why: Native apps respect accessibility zoom and text size. Blocking pinch fails WCAG 1.4.4 and axe. The usual reason to add maximum-scale=1 is to stop iOS focus-zoom, and that is better solved with 16px fields.
items.how:
<!-- NEVER: axe 'meta-viewport' (critical, WCAG 1.4.4) fails when maximum-scale < 2 or user-scalable=no;
     'meta-viewport-large' (best practice) flags maximum-scale < 5 -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no">

<!-- Instead: the baseline meta + -->
<style>
  html { touch-action: manipulation; }                 /* no double-tap zoom, pinch stays */
  @media (pointer: coarse) { input, textarea, select, [contenteditable] { font-size: 16px !important; } } /* no focus zoom */
  .drawing-canvas { touch-action: none; }             /* only gesture surfaces opt out */
</style>
items.support: iOS 10+ ignores user-scalable=no and min/maximum-scale for user pinch, but maximum-scale=1 still stops the automatic focus zoom (the trap). Chrome, Firefox and Samsung on Android honour them, so pinch zoom is really blocked there.
items.gotchas: Code that sizes the app from visualViewport must multiply heights by visualViewport.scale, or pinch-zoom shrinks the layout (Yurt). Run axe on every E2E page (Yurt's checkPage runs axe + html-validate), so a regression in the meta tag fails CI.

items.title: Stop iOS focus-zoom: 16px form fields on coarse pointers only
items.what: iOS Safari zooms the page into any focused field whose computed font-size is below 16px. Force 16px on touch-first devices and keep the compact desktop size elsewhere.
items.why: Focus zoom pans the page sideways and leaves it zoomed after blur, so the user has to pinch out. It is one of the most recognisable 'this is a website' tells on iPhone.
items.support: This is the behaviour of every iOS/iPadOS WebKit browser, in a tab and in a home-screen app. (pointer: coarse) works everywhere: Chrome 41 / Android 50, Safari 9, Firefox 64.
items.gotchas: Applies to contenteditable editors and search fields in headers too. iPad with a trackpad still reports a coarse primary pointer, so the rule stays on (correct, because iPadOS also zooms). Faking smaller text with transform: scale() is fragile. Don't fix it with maximum-scale=1: that blocks pinch-zoom on Android and fails axe. A 16px line-height can make fields taller, so check the composer height.
sources: Yurt: packages/ui/tokens/base.css, AGENTS.md (iOS zooms into focused fields under 16px)

items.title: touch-action: manipulation on the root
items.what: One line that disables double-tap-to-zoom (and any residual tap delay) everywhere while keeping panning and pinch-zoom.
items.why: Double-tapping a button or a message quickly zooms the page. Native apps never do that.
items.how:
html { touch-action: manipulation; }          /* pan + pinch-zoom allowed, double-tap zoom off */
.signature-pad, .map-canvas { touch-action: none; } /* custom gesture surfaces */
.swipe-row { touch-action: pan-y pinch-zoom; }        /* horizontal swipe handled in JS, vertical scroll native */
items.support: Chrome 36, Safari iOS 9.3 / macOS 13, Firefox 52, Samsung 3. Universal.
items.gotchas: touch-action is not inherited, but the effective value is the intersection of the element and all its ancestors. Setting it on html therefore covers the whole page, and descendants can only restrict it further (they cannot re-enable double-tap zoom). It does not stop iOS focus-zoom (use 16px fields).

items.title: text-size-adjust: 100% (no landscape/font-boosting inflation)
items.what: Turn off mobile text-inflation heuristics so type renders at the sizes you designed, in both orientations.
items.why: iOS Safari enlarges text on rotation to landscape, and Android 'font boosting' enlarges some text blocks. The result is inconsistent sizes and text that jumps on rotate, which native apps never show.
items.support: Chrome/Edge/Samsung 54+ unprefixed (matters on Android). Safari iOS: -webkit- prefix only. Firefox Android: -webkit- (49+). Desktop Safari and Firefox: no-op. BCD marks it experimental.
items.gotchas: Use 100%, not none: none has historically interfered with user text zoom in some browsers. It does not block user/OS accessibility text scaling. If you opt into <meta name="text-scale" content="scale"> (Chrome 146+), the browser disables autosizing anyway.

items.title: Dynamic viewport units (svh / lvh / dvh) and the 100vh bug
items.what: On mobile, 100vh equals the LARGE viewport (browser bars retracted), so it overflows the visible area while the toolbar shows. svh = bars expanded (smallest), lvh = bars retracted (largest), dvh = the current size.
items.why: A '100vh' screen whose bottom buttons hide behind Safari/Chrome bars, or a hero that jumps as the bar collapses, is a classic web tell.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 108, Safari 15.4 (macOS + iOS), Firefox 101, Samsung 21. Baseline. In installed apps (standalone, no browser bars) sv = lv = dv.
items.gotchas: dvh changes while toolbars collapse during document scroll, which causes relayout and content shifts. Don't size content in a scrolling page with dvh; use svh. None of the units follow the iOS keyboard (the iOS layout viewport doesn't resize). On Android with interactive-widget=resizes-content, all of them shrink with the keyboard. Yurt uses height:100% (not dvh, not visualViewport) as the default because in an installed iOS app the visual viewport can be short by the status bar while CSS 100% is right. Safari 26.0 showed a bottom gap with viewport-sized fixed containers under Liquid Glass; Safari 26.1 fixed it. Drop -webkit-fill-available and JS '--vh' hacks for toolbar handling.

items.title: Locked app shell with in-flow bars and inner scroll containers
items.what: The document never scrolls (html/body height 100%, overflow hidden). Header, tab bar and composer are grid rows, not position:fixed, and each pane is its own scroll container.
items.why: This is how native apps look: chrome stays put and panes scroll independently. It avoids the whole page rubber-banding, address-bar resize jumps, fixed-element jitter (including iOS 26 fixed bottom bars landing mid-screen), and makes keyboard handling a matter of resizing one box.
items.how:
…
…
…
html { height: 100%; } body { height: var(--app-height, 100%); margin: 0; overflow: hidden; overscroll-behavior: none; } .app { height: 100%; display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto minmax(0, 1fr) auto; /* minmax(0, …) or the row grows to its content and never scrolls */ padding: var(--safe-top) var(--safe-right) var(--safe-bottom) var(--safe-left); } .scroller { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior-y: contain; } /* flex version: .pane { flex: 1; min-height: 0; overflow-y: auto; } */
items.support: All engines. iOS has respected overflow:hidden on body for touch scrolling of the main frame since WebKit bug 153852 was fixed (2019).
items.gotchas: This is a trade-off, so pick per product. In a browser tab, the Safari/Chrome toolbar never minimizes. iOS tap-the-status-bar-to-scroll-to-top only scrolls the document, so inner scrollers lose it (a JS workaround needs a 1px document scroll hack, or you accept the loss). Chrome Android pull-to-refresh only acts on the document. Content and marketing sites should keep document scrolling. overflow:hidden does NOT stop programmatic scrolling of html/body (scrollIntoView, focus, anchors), so see the focused-field item. 1fr alone means minmax(auto, 1fr), which is the classic 'inner div won't scroll' bug.

items.title: Safe-area tokens: env(safe-area-inset-*) with fallbacks and max()
items.what: Expose the four insets as CSS custom properties (overridable from JS), pad chrome with max(design padding, inset), and let backgrounds bleed to the edges.
items.why: Content stays clear of the notch/Dynamic Island, home indicator, rounded corners and landscape cutouts, while bars and backgrounds reach the physical edge the way native apps do.
items.support: env(): Chrome 69, Safari 11.1 / iOS 11.3, Firefox 65. Non-zero values need viewport-fit=cover (iOS; Chrome Android 135+ edge-to-edge). Insets are 0 on desktop.
items.gotchas: Use PHYSICAL left/right for insets: the cutout side flips with landscape direction, and logical padding-inline would mis-map in RTL. env() is not allowed in media queries. Values differ between a Safari tab and the installed app, and change as toolbars move, so test both. Tokens let JS override them: Yurt sets --safe-bottom: 0 while the iOS keyboard covers the home indicator. With black-translucent installed iOS apps, --safe-top is the status bar height. Always pass a 0px fallback so calc() stays valid.

items.title: Android edge-to-edge: safe-area-max-inset-* for stable bottom bars
items.what: Since Chrome 135 on Android (gesture navigation, phones first), viewport-fit=cover pages draw behind the gesture bar once Chrome's bottom 'chin' retracts. safe-area-inset-bottom then changes as the user scrolls; safe-area-max-inset-bottom is constant.
items.why: Fixed bottom CTAs and tab bars stop jittering up and down with the browser UI and never sit under the gesture handle.
items.support: safe-area-max-inset-*: Chromium 135+ on Android only. Not in Safari or Firefox; unknown env names fall back to the second argument. MDN documents it, but BCD has no entry yet.
items.gotchas: At launch this applied only to gesture navigation on phones, not 3-button navigation or tablets. Without viewport-fit=cover nothing changes. In a locked shell where the document doesn't scroll, the chin rarely retracts, but test with gesture nav anyway.

items.title: Know the three keyboard resize behaviors per platform
items.what: resizes-visual (default everywhere): the visual viewport shrinks, the layout viewport and vh don't, fixed elements stay put and get covered. resizes-content: both shrink (Android opt-in). overlays-content: nothing resizes (VirtualKeyboard API or meta). iOS pans the page instead of resizing it.
items.why: Every 'keyboard covers my input / composer floats mid-screen / page jumped' bug comes from assuming one model. Native apps resize their content area to the space above the keyboard.
items.support: resizes-visual is the default in Safari iOS / iPadOS and every iOS browser, Chrome Android 108+, Firefox Android 132+, ChromeOS and Windows. visualViewport: Chrome 61, Safari 13, Firefox 91 (Android 68).
items.gotchas: There is no standard 'keyboard opened' event; visualViewport resize is the signal. On iOS it fires once at the end of the keyboard animation, so layout snaps rather than animates (only the Chromium VirtualKeyboard geometrychange event lets you track it). focusin fires before the keyboard is up, so don't measure then. iPad floating or split keyboards and hardware keyboards (shortcut bar only) barely shrink the visual viewport, which is fine with the threshold. On Android with resizes-content, the function above returns false because the layout already fits. Programmatic focus() opens the iOS keyboard only inside a user gesture. enterkeyhint/inputmode/autocomplete shape the keyboard itself.

items.title: iOS keyboard: size and move the shell to the visual viewport, only while a keyboard is up
items.what: iOS keeps the layout and pans over it when the keyboard opens. Drive --app-height (visible height x scale), --app-top (where iOS panned to) and --safe-bottom: 0 from visualViewport, but only while the covered height exceeds a keyboard threshold. Otherwise clear them and let CSS 100% stand.
items.why: The composer sits right on top of the keyboard and the header stays visible, like a native chat app. Without it the composer hides under the keyboard, or floats above it with a gap below.
items.support: Needed on Safari iOS/iPadOS and every iOS browser, in a tab and in a home-screen app. It is a harmless no-op on Android with resizes-content (the layout shrinks too, so the difference stays under the threshold) and on desktop. visualViewport: Safari 13+.
items.gotchas: Don't set --app-height from visualViewport all the time: in an installed iOS app the visual viewport can be shorter than the layout by the status bar (e.g. 797 vs 844), which leaves a gap at the bottom, while CSS 100% is right. Use pageTop (scroll + offsetTop), not offsetTop alone, because iOS scrolls the layout viewport even with overflow:hidden. Listen to scroll as well as resize. A transform on body makes body the containing block of every position:fixed descendant (intended here: body is the viewport-sized shell) and creates a stacking context. iOS 26.0 had a bug where visualViewport.offsetTop sometimes wasn't reset after the keyboard closed, misplacing fixed headers; re-syncing on scroll helps. When Safari ships interactive-widget, this code stays inert because the threshold check clears the vars.

items.title: position:fixed / sticky with the iOS keyboard (and the iOS 26 regressions)
items.what: On iOS, fixed elements are laid out against the layout viewport, which doesn't shrink for the keyboard. Fixed bottom bars end up under the keyboard or float mid-page while it pans, and after dismissal fixed elements can stay offset.
items.why: A tab bar or 'Send' button jumping, floating or hiding behind the keyboard is an immediate web tell.
items.support: The problem: Safari iOS/iPadOS and all iOS browsers. Safari 26 (Liquid Glass) added fixed/sticky misplacement reports; 26.1 fixed a bottom gap for viewport-sized fixed containers. Android with resizes-content moves fixed bottom bars above the keyboard by itself.
items.gotchas: The innerHeight/offsetTop formula is the widely used community approach, but its semantics have shifted between iOS releases (toolbar states, 26.0 offsetTop bug), so verify on a device. The focusout reset only makes sense when the document is never meant to scroll. On iOS 26 Safari, 'bottom: 0' in a tab sits relative to the area under the floating Liquid Glass toolbar; keeping bars in-flow in a locked 100% shell with safe-area padding is the robust fix.

items.title: VirtualKeyboard API (Chromium): overlaysContent, geometrychange, keyboard-inset-*
items.what: Opt out of the browser's keyboard resizing and lay out around the keyboard yourself, in CSS (env(keyboard-inset-*)) or JS (boundingRect + geometrychange). Add virtualkeyboardpolicy="manual" to show or hide it on your terms for contenteditable.
items.why: Gives precise, animation-friendly control (e.g. a keyboard-height grid row, an emoji panel that swaps with the keyboard, a dual-screen device where the keyboard covers one screen) instead of a full relayout.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 94+ (Android and touch ChromeOS/Windows), Samsung 17, WebView 94. No Safari (iOS/macOS), no Firefox. Experimental; secure context only.
items.gotchas: Feature-detect and keep the iOS visualViewport path. keyboard-inset-* are 0 unless overlaysContent is true. Setting it is the scripted equivalent of interactive-widget=overlays-content, so the browser no longer guarantees the focused field is visible (use scroll-padding or scroll it yourself). show() needs a focused editable element with virtualkeyboardpolicy=manual and may require user activation (verify). Not in TypeScript's lib.dom, hence the declaration.

items.title: Keep the focused field visible without moving the locked shell
items.what: After the keyboard resize, scroll ONLY the pane's scroller so the focused field is visible. Focus programmatically with preventScroll, and use scroll-padding so browser-initiated scrolls leave room for sticky headers and the composer.
items.why: Native apps scroll the field into view inside the list. Browsers' scrollIntoView/focus also scroll html/body and every overflow:hidden ancestor, which shifts the whole shell ('the app jumped up and stayed there').
items.support: getBoundingClientRect/scrollTop: universal. focus({preventScroll}): Chrome 64, Safari 15 / iOS 15.5, Firefox 68 (BCD lists Chrome/Firefox Android as unsupported, so verify). scrollIntoView container option: Chrome/Edge 140+ only. scroll-padding applied to scrollIntoView: Safari 14.1 / iOS 14.5+.
items.gotchas: overflow:hidden only blocks user scrolling; programmatic scrolls still move html/body. overflow:clip on non-root wrappers blocks programmatic scrolling too, but on html/body it propagates to the viewport as hidden. Measure after visualViewport resize, not on focus. Prefer block:'nearest'; BCD notes older Safari lacked 'center'. scrollIntoView now returns a Promise in Chrome 150+ only. The container option is not in TypeScript's lib.dom, hence the augmentation.

items.title: Auto-growing composer with field-sizing: content
items.what: A textarea that grows with its text up to a few lines, then scrolls internally, with no JS.
items.why: Native message composers grow line by line. Fixed-height textareas with an inner scrollbar, or JS height jank on every keystroke, feel webby.
items.support: Chrome 123, Safari 26.2 (macOS + iOS), Firefox 152, Samsung 27. All current engines. lh unit: Chrome 109, Safari 16.4, Firefox 120.
items.gotchas: Scope it: field-sizing also changes <input>/<select> widths. Put the composer in an auto grid row of the shell so growth shrinks the message list instead of pushing under the keyboard. An empty field sizes to its placeholder. Keep the JS fallback until your support floor includes Safari 26.2 (Yurt's Composer still uses the scrollHeight approach).

items.title: Chat/timeline lists that open and stay at the bottom (column-reverse wrapper)
items.what: Make the scroller a flex column-reverse with ONE child that holds messages in chronological DOM order. The scroll origin is then the bottom: it opens at the newest message, stays pinned when the scroller shrinks (keyboard, growing composer), and loading older history above doesn't move the view.
items.why: Native chat opens at the latest message with no visible scroll-to-bottom flash, and the last message stays above the composer when the keyboard opens.
items.how: .log { display: flex; flex-direction: column-reverse; overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior-y: contain; min-height: 0; } const log = document.querySelector('.log'); // scrollTop is 0 at the bottom and negative above it const distanceFromBottom = (el: HTMLElement) => -el.scrollTop; const showJumpToLatest = (el: HTMLElement) => distanceFromBottom(el) > 160; const toLatest = (el: HTMLElement) => el.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches ? 'auto' : 'smooth' });
items.support: All current engines. Chrome 81+ uses spec-negative scrollTop for column-reverse; Firefox fixed scrolling of column-reverse containers in 81; Safari has always used negative offsets.
items.gotchas: Code or libraries that assume scrollTop >= 0 break. While the user is scrolled up, a new message at the bottom can shift what they're reading. Verify per engine and compensate if needed. The single inner wrapper keeps reading/Tab order chronological; reversing the DOM itself would make screen readers read newest-first. Alternative with a normal column (Yurt's current approach): scroll to scrollHeight on open, keep an 'at bottom' flag (within about 160px), re-pin on new messages and on ResizeObserver(scroller) only when the flag is set. The overflow-anchor pin trick (all children overflow-anchor:none, a 1px last child overflow-anchor:auto) now works in Safari 27+ too.

items.title: Scroll anchoring (overflow-anchor), now in every engine
items.what: The browser keeps the content you're looking at still when content above it is inserted or resized (older messages, late images, banners). Exclude transient rows from being chosen as anchors.
items.why: Content jumping while you read is a strong web tell; native list views keep their position.
items.support: Chrome 56, Firefox 66, Safari 27.0 (macOS + iOS, Sept 2026, Safari's first support).
items.gotchas: Anchoring doesn't help when the scroller itself shrinks (keyboard): use the column-reverse list or re-pin with a ResizeObserver. Users on iOS < 27 still exist, so keep the fallback within your support window. Give images width/height or aspect-ratio so content below doesn't jump either.

items.title: overscroll-behavior: no page rubber-band, no accidental pull-to-refresh, no scroll chaining
items.what: Use none on the root to kill page bounce/glow, pull-to-refresh and overscroll navigation, and contain on inner scrollers so reaching the end of a list doesn't scroll the page or panel behind it.
items.why: Pulling a chat list down and reloading the whole app, or a sheet's scroll leaking into the page behind it, never happens in native apps.
items.how:
html, body { overscroll-behavior: none; }               /* no root bounce/glow, no pull-to-refresh, no overscroll nav */
.scroller  { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior-y: contain; } /* no chaining; local bounce kept */
.carousel, .tabs-strip { overscroll-behavior-x: contain; }       /* horizontal edges don't trigger back/forward */
items.support: Chrome 63, Firefox 59, Safari 16 (macOS + iOS), Edge 18. Chrome 144 and Firefox 150 also apply it to NON-scrollable scroll containers (overflow:hidden, or auto without overflow); Safari still only when the box actually overflows.
items.gotchas: contain stops chaining and browser actions but keeps the element's own bounce/glow; none removes those too. Chrome Android shows pull-to-refresh in installed standalone PWAs as well, so disable it on html and provide your own refresh affordance (or keep it on content sites). iOS: overscroll-behavior on the root does not reliably stop the main frame's rubber-band (WKWebView ignores it); the locked shell is what keeps the app from bouncing. overscroll-behavior-x does not reliably block two-finger history swipes on Windows Chrome, and the iOS/Android system back gestures can't be blocked by a page.

items.title: Scroll lock under modals and sheets in CSS
items.what: Stop the page scrolling behind a modal <dialog> or bottom sheet without JS scroll-lock libraries.
items.why: Background content scrolling under a sheet is a classic web tell, and JS locks (body position:fixed) lose scroll position and flash.
items.how:
dialog { overscroll-behavior: contain; }                          /* UA gives modal dialogs overflow:auto */
dialog::backdrop { overflow: hidden; overscroll-behavior: contain; } /* backdrop becomes a non-scrollable scroll container that stops chaining */
html:has(dialog:modal) { overflow: hidden; }                       /* fallback for engines without the 144 behavior */
.sheet-body { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain; }
html { scrollbar-gutter: stable; }                                   /* desktop: no layout shift when the scrollbar disappears */
items.support: The pure-CSS dialog lock works in Chrome 144+ and Firefox 150+. Safari needs the :has() fallback (:has 15.4, dialog 15.4).
items.gotchas: In a locked app shell the document never scrolls, so this matters mostly for document-scroll pages and for sheets over inner scrollers. On iOS, html overflow:hidden is intentionally not enforced in some states (Safari with collapsed toolbar; historically standalone), so test on a device. If you must use the position:fixed body hack, save and restore scrollY.

items.title: Delete obsolete iOS scrolling/height hacks
items.what: Remove -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch, height: -webkit-fill-available, JS '--vh = innerHeight/100' toolbar hacks, touchmove preventDefault no-bounce scripts and window.orientation listeners.
items.why: They are now no-ops or cause bugs: extra stacking contexts and rendering glitches, non-passive touch listeners that make scrolling janky, and stale sizes.
items.support: Momentum scrolling has been the default for overflow scrollers since iOS 13. The property is gone from MDN/BCD. window.orientation and orientationchange are deprecated (mobile-only).
items.gotchas: A JS-computed height is still legitimate for one case: the iOS keyboard (visualViewport item), not toolbars. Search the codebase and CSS-in-JS for these strings; component libraries often still ship them.

items.title: Scroll-snap pagers and carousels, with scrollend
items.what: Native-feeling swipe pagers (onboarding, image galleries, swipeable tabs) built on CSS scroll snap, with the page index derived on scrollend.
items.why: You get real momentum, rubber-banding and accessibility for free, unlike JS transform carousels that fight the finger.
items.support: scroll-snap-type/align: Chrome 69, Safari 11, Firefox 68 (desktop fully 99). scroll-snap-stop: Chrome 75, Safari 15, Firefox 103. scrollend: Chrome 114, Firefox 109, Safari 26.2. scrollsnapchange/scrollsnapchanging events: Chromium 129+ only. ::scroll-marker / ::scroll-button carousels: Chromium 135+ only. scroll-initial-target: Chromium 133+ only.
items.gotchas: mandatory snapping with items taller than the scrollport can trap users; use proximity for vertical lists. Hidden scrollbars need visible prev/next buttons for mouse users on (pointer: fine), who have no horizontal wheel. Keep real tab buttons for a11y when the pager is a tab view. setPage is your state callback.

items.title: Desktop scrollbars: stable gutter, thin themed bars, hidden on strips
items.what: Reserve scrollbar space so layouts don't shift when content starts overflowing, make scrollbars thin and themed, and hide them on horizontal chip strips and pagers.
items.why: Layout jumping by 15px when a list grows, and fat grey scrollbars inside a dark app, are desktop web tells.
items.how:
.scroller { scrollbar-gutter: stable; scrollbar-width: thin; scrollbar-color: var(--scroll-thumb) transparent; }
.chips, .pager { scrollbar-width: none; } /* still scrollable by touch, trackpad, keyboard */
items.support: scrollbar-gutter: Chrome 94, Firefox 97, Safari 18.2. scrollbar-width: Chrome 121, Firefox 64, Safari 18.2. scrollbar-color: Chrome 121, Firefox 64, Safari 26.2. Android WebView: no.
items.gotchas: In Chromium, setting scrollbar-width or scrollbar-color on an element disables its ::-webkit-scrollbar styling. Gutters do nothing with overlay scrollbars (mobile, macOS default), which is harmless. Hidden scrollbars need another affordance on pointer: fine (arrows, edge fades).

items.title: No sideways wobble: overflow-x: clip and min-width: 0
items.what: Clip stray horizontal overflow without creating a scroll container, and let flex/grid children shrink so long words, URLs and code don't widen the page.
items.why: A page that pans a few pixels sideways under the thumb is an instant web tell; native views never pan horizontally.
items.support: overflow: clip: Chrome 90, Safari 16, Firefox 81.
items.gotchas: overflow-x: hidden makes the element a scroll container: it breaks position:sticky in descendants and can still be scrolled programmatically. clip does neither. On html/body, clip propagates to the viewport and acts like hidden. Find culprits in devtools: elements whose getBoundingClientRect().right is greater than document.documentElement.clientWidth.

items.title: Sticky section headers with scroll-padding and a stuck state
items.what: Sticky headers inside the pane's scroller, scroll-padding so focus, anchor and scrollIntoView targets land below them, and a 'stuck' style (hairline/shadow) via scroll-state container queries where supported.
items.why: This matches native grouped lists (contacts, settings, day separators), where headers pin and gain a separator only while pinned.
items.support: position: sticky: universal (Safari 13 unprefixed). scroll-padding: Chrome 69, Firefox 68, Safari 14.1 / iOS 14.5 for scrollIntoView. scroll-state() queries: Chromium 133+ only (stuck/snapped/scrollable; scrolled 144+); elsewhere no shadow, which is acceptable as progressive enhancement.
items.gotchas: Sticky silently fails if any ancestor between it and the scroller has overflow hidden/auto (use clip). Give the sticky bar an opaque background. Cross-engine fallback for the stuck style: an IntersectionObserver on a 1px sentinel above the header.

items.title: Collapsing or hide-on-scroll headers without scroll listeners
items.what: Shrink or tint a header as content scrolls (scroll-driven animations), or hide it while scrolling down and show it on scroll-up (scroll-state 'scrolled').
items.why: This gives iOS-style large-title collapse and app bars that get out of the way, with no main-thread scroll handlers (which cause jank).
items.support: animation-timeline / scroll(): Chrome 115, Safari 26 (macOS + iOS), Firefox only behind a flag (preview). scroll-state(scrolled): Chromium 144+ only.
items.gotchas: animation-timeline must come after the animation shorthand, which resets it. Animate cheap properties (colors, shadow, transform) rather than font-size/padding, which trigger layout. Don't hide headers that contain the focused element. A JS fallback for direction needs a passive scroll listener with rAF.

items.title: Scroll restoration for inner scrollers (Navigation API)
items.what: Browsers restore only the document's scroll. In a shell with inner scrollers, save each view's scrollTop per history entry and restore it on back/forward after the view renders; new navigations start at the top.
items.why: Native back navigation returns you exactly where you were in the list. Landing at the top, or briefly at the wrong offset, feels webby.
items.support: Navigation API: Chrome/Edge 102 (intercept/scroll 105), Safari 26.2 (macOS + iOS), Firefox 147. Baseline as of 2026. history.scrollRestoration: universal (Safari 11, Chrome 46, Firefox 46).
items.gotchas: Restore only after data and rows exist (virtual lists need their data first). Persist the map to sessionStorage if you want positions to survive reloads. For tab bars, keep each tab's view mounted (hidden) like native tab controllers, which is cheaper and more exact than restoring. Re-tapping the active tab should scroll that tab to the top (native convention). Guard with 'navigation' in window if you support Safari < 26.2.

items.title: iOS home-screen status bar: default/black vs black-translucent
items.what: apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style decides whether an installed iOS web app starts below an opaque status bar (default/black) or draws under it (black-translucent, white status text, content needs top safe-area padding).
items.why: Content under a translucent status bar looks native, but on iOS 26+ it now comes with sizing gaps and a Liquid Glass blur over the top of the page. An opaque bar is the predictable choice.
items.how:
<!-- Predictable since iOS 26: opaque bar, web view starts below it, env(safe-area-inset-top) = 0 -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="default">

<!-- Or draw under the status bar (needs viewport-fit=cover) -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="black-translucent">
<style>
  .topbar { padding-top: var(--safe-top); }
  html { height: 100%; } body { height: var(--app-height, 100%); } /* not visualViewport/dvh by default */
</style>
items.support: Installed home-screen web apps on iOS/iPadOS only; a Safari tab ignores it. Since iOS 26, every site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default (users can turn 'Open as Web App' off).
items.gotchas: iOS reads the value at install time: after changing it, users must remove and re-add the app. Field reports from Sept 2026 (iOS 26 and 27.0): with black-translucent, the standalone viewport can be one status bar (~59-60pt) short, leaving a band at the top or bottom, and a Liquid Glass edge blur covers about the top 110px, obscuring header text. Several teams switched to black/default. Yurt keeps black-translucent and avoids the gap by keeping CSS 100% heights and only using visualViewport while a keyboard is up (the visual viewport is short by the status bar, e.g. 797 vs 844). black-translucent status text is white, which is unreadable on light themes. theme-color is only used by installed web apps from Safari 26 (BCD). These are device-tested reports rather than Apple documentation, so verify on current iOS.

items.title: Safari 26+ toolbar tinting and full-screen dims come from edge-hugging fixed/sticky elements
items.what: Since Safari 26 (Liquid Glass), a browser tab ignores theme-color. Safari tints its top and bottom bars by sampling a fixed or sticky element at the viewport edge, falling back to the html/body background. Full-screen dims reach the bars only as position:fixed; inset:0.
items.why: Mismatched white or black bands around your header, or a modal scrim that leaves Safari's bars bright, make the page look like a website inside a browser rather than an app.
items.how:
html, body { background-color: var(--surface-page); }                               /* fallback sample */
.topbar { position: sticky; top: 0; background-color: var(--surface-bar); }        /* opaque, full width → tints the top */
.scrim  { position: fixed; inset: 0; background-color: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4); }          /* dims Safari's bars too */
/* not: position:absolute scrims, height:100vh scrims, or gradients/background-image as the bar color */
items.support: Safari 26+ on iOS/iPadOS in a browser tab (and macOS for the top). Needs viewport-fit=cover. Installed web apps still use theme-color (BCD: from Safari 26, theme-color only for installed web apps).
items.gotchas: The heuristics are undocumented and were reverse-engineered on iOS 26.5 and 27.0: the topmost fixed/sticky layer is hit-tested at the edge centre about 4px in, and must be at least ~90% wide, more than 10px deep and at opacity 0.1 or above, with its OWN background-color. Empty full-width pointer-events:none overlays on top block the sample. A fixed toast at the top edge can retint the bar while visible. Re-test on each iOS release.

items.title: Orientation changes: respond, don't lock
items.what: Adapt to rotation with media queries and screen.orientation's change event, give landscape phones a compact layout, and lock orientation only for fullscreen media or games where supported.
items.why: Native apps reflow cleanly on rotation. Clipped headers in landscape phone mode and stale measurements after rotating look broken.
items.support: ScreenOrientation + change event: Chrome 38, Firefox 43, Safari 16.4. orientation media query: universal. lock(): Chrome Android 38+ (generally needs fullscreen), Firefox 144 (BCD), not Safari/iOS; desktop Chrome throws NotSupportedError. window.orientation/orientationchange: deprecated.
items.gotchas: WCAG 1.3.4 forbids restricting orientation unless essential, and tablets, foldables and desktop windows rotate or resize freely. Safe-area left/right swap with landscape direction. Manifest 'orientation' for installed apps is honoured by Chromium; don't rely on it on iOS (verify). Older TypeScript lib.dom versions dropped ScreenOrientation.lock (TS 7's lib.dom has it).

items.title: Foldables: Viewport Segments API (dual-pane across the hinge)
items.what: Detect a viewport split by a fold or hinge and place panes on either side of it, using media features, env(viewport-segment-*) and window.viewport.segments.
items.why: Native foldable apps put list and detail on separate halves and never draw text across the hinge.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 138+ (Android and desktop), Samsung 30, WebView 138. No Safari, no Firefox. Experimental.
items.gotchas: On single-screen devices the media features are false and the env() values undefined, so always write a one-segment layout first. Segments change on fold, unfold and rotate, so re-evaluate on resize. Guard for both null and one-element arrays. DevTools can emulate dual-screen devices. MDN's example uses grid-column with env widths; use grid-template-columns as above.

items.title: Device Posture API (folded vs continuous)
items.what: Know whether a foldable is flat ('continuous') or half-folded ('folded', book or laptop posture), via a media query and navigator.devicePosture.
items.why: Enables native-style tabletop modes, e.g. video on the top half and controls on the bottom half when the phone is propped open.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 132+ (BCD lists desktop and Android), Samsung 16.2. Safari iOS 27 behind a flag only. No Firefox. Experimental.
items.gotchas: Non-foldables always report continuous. DevTools can't emulate half-folded. Combine with viewport segments to know where the fold is.

items.title: Container queries for components that adapt to their pane
items.what: Components respond to the width of the pane they're in (sidebar, main pane, split view, Stage Manager window) rather than the screen, much like native size classes.
items.why: The same message row or card looks right in a 320px sidebar and a 900px detail pane. Screen-width breakpoints break as soon as you add split views.
items.support: Size queries and cq units: Chrome 105, Safari 16, Firefox 110. Style queries for custom properties: Chrome 111, Safari 18, Firefox 151. scroll-state queries: Chromium only.
items.gotchas: inline-size containment means the container can't take its width from its children, so shrink-to-fit containers collapse. Put container-type on panes and grid cells with definite widths. container-type: size also needs an explicit height. A container can't query itself; style its descendants. In Safari the document element can't be a style-query container.

items.title: Large screens: list-detail split view by width, not device
items.what: From about 768px wide, show list and detail side by side with the selection in the URL. Below that, push detail as a full screen with a back button.
items.why: A stretched phone layout on an iPad or desktop window is a strong web tell. Native tablet apps use split views.
items.support: Universal. Media range syntax: Chrome 104, Safari 16.4, Firefox 102.
items.gotchas: iPadOS Safari sends a Mac user agent, and Split View, Slide Over and Stage Manager windows can be any width, so decide by width (and pointer), never by UA or device. Keep the same URL in both modes (route = selection) so rotating or resizing keeps state. Show back buttons only in the stacked mode. Landscape phones (max-height: 500px) are not tablets.

items.title: Desktop installed PWAs: Window Controls Overlay (titlebar-area-*)
items.what: Installed desktop PWAs can draw into the title bar area next to the OS window buttons, like native desktop apps (Slack, VS Code), with draggable regions.
items.why: It removes the generic browser-like title bar strip above your app's own header.
items.support: Chrome/Edge desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux; Linux since 93) for installed PWAs only. API objects 105+. No Android, Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: Users can toggle the overlay off (visible becomes false, env fallbacks apply), so the layout must work both ways. Draggable regions swallow clicks, so mark every control no-drag. BCD lists only the -webkit-app-region spelling; keep it (unprefixed app-region support is unverified).

items.title: Honor OS text size: <meta name="text-scale"> (Chrome) and Dynamic Type (iOS)
items.what: Opt the root font size into the OS/browser text-size setting so rem-based UI scales the way native apps do with system font size.
items.why: Native apps grow with the user's accessibility text setting, while web apps usually ignore it on mobile.
items.how:
<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">
<style>
  html { font-size: 100%; }   /* never px on :root; size type and spacing in rem/em */
  /* iOS WebKit: Dynamic Type for web content (non-standard; verify sizes) */
  @media (pointer: coarse) { @supports (font: -apple-system-body) { html { font: -apple-system-body; font-family: var(--font-body); } } }
</style>
items.support: text-scale meta: Chrome/Edge 146+ (Android and desktop). env(preferred-text-scale): Chrome 138+, Samsung 30. Neither in Safari or Firefox. -apple-system-body: long-standing WebKit on iOS (non-standard).
items.gotchas: Opting in means supporting 200-300%+ text; test layouts at those sizes. Don't use both the meta and env(preferred-text-scale), or text scales twice. The meta also disables mobile text-autosizing heuristics. -apple-system-body sets a different base size per device and setting and can conflict with a fixed design scale, so treat it as experimental.

items.title: content-visibility: auto for long lists
items.what: Skip layout and paint for off-screen rows in long chats and feeds, with remembered intrinsic sizes.
items.why: Scrolling stays at 60/120fps on mid-range phones. Scroll jank is a top 'web app' tell.
items.how: .message { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 64px; } /* 'auto' remembers the last rendered height */
items.support: Chrome 85, Firefox 125, Safari 18.
items.gotchas: Estimated heights can nudge the scroll position as rows render; scroll anchoring (Safari 27+) or the column-reverse list hides this. Find-in-page and the accessibility tree still see the content. For thousands of rows, use virtualization. Don't apply it to sticky headers or rows being animated.
